name: DRESS syndrome
aliases: drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

clinicalPearls: Onset is classically delayed, typically 2-8 weeks after starting the culprit drug, distinguishing it from more immediate hypersensitivity reactions.
Look for the triad of fever, widespread morbilliform (often confluent and edematous) rash, and facial edema, especially periorbital swelling.
Systemic involvement is the hallmark: lymphadenopathy plus at least one internal organ (liver most common, also kidney, lung, heart) helps separate DRESS from simple drug rash.
Peripheral eosinophilia and/or atypical lymphocytosis on blood smear strongly support the diagnosis but may lag behind skin findings.
Common culprits include aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, and certain antibiotics — always take a careful medication history covering the prior 2 months.
Symptoms can worsen for days to weeks even after the offending drug is stopped, and relapses/flares are common during the recovery phase.
Human herpesvirus-6 reactivation is frequently detected during the illness and may contribute to prolonged or relapsing disease course.
Cross-reactivity exists among structurally related anticonvulsants, so the entire drug class should generally be avoided going forward.
harrison.pathophysiology: DRESS is a severe, delayed T-cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity reaction, thought to arise from impaired drug detoxification pathways or specific HLA associations that lead to a robust immune response against drug-modified proteins. The resulting systemic activation of eosinophils and lymphocytes drives multi-organ inflammation. Reactivation of latent herpesviruses, particularly HHV-6, is commonly observed and may amplify and prolong the immune response, contributing to the characteristic waxing-waning course.
additionalDifferentials: Viral exanthem (e.g., EBV, CMV, HHV-6 primary infection)
Autoimmune connective tissue disease with rash and organ involvement
additionalInvestigations: Complete blood count with differential — assesses eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytosis
Liver function tests — screens for hepatitis, the most common visceral involvement
Serum creatinine and urinalysis — evaluates renal involvement
Chest imaging — assesses for pulmonary infiltrates or pneumonitis
Skin biopsy — supports diagnosis and helps exclude other severe cutaneous adverse reactions
HHV-6 (and other herpesvirus) serology/PCR — assesses viral reactivation contributing to disease course
Cardiac enzymes/echocardiography if myocarditis suspected — detects cardiac involvement
Thyroid function tests at follow-up — late autoimmune thyroiditis can occur after recovery
redFlags: Evidence of fulminant hepatitis or rising transaminases suggesting hepatic failure
Signs of myocarditis (chest pain, arrhythmia, heart failure) or interstitial pneumonitis
Acute kidney injury with rising creatinine
Rapidly progressive skin involvement raising concern for overlap with SJS/TEN
pitfalls: Attributing the rash only to the most recently started drug while missing a culprit introduced weeks earlier due to the characteristic delayed onset.
Discontinuing suspected culprit and expecting immediate improvement — worsening despite drug withdrawal is common and should not prompt reinstatement.
Underestimating disease severity because eosinophilia or organ involvement may be absent or delayed at initial presentation.
Failing to screen for and monitor internal organ involvement once the skin findings are recognized, since mortality is driven by visceral disease, not the rash itself.
harrison.prognosis: DRESS carries a mortality risk of roughly 5-10%, primarily related to fulminant hepatic, cardiac, or pulmonary involvement. Even after recovery, patients can develop delayed autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes, or other autoimmune conditions over the following months to years, warranting longitudinal follow-up.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Cutaneous Drug Reactions
management: Immediately and permanently withdraw the culprit drug and avoid structurally related agents such as cross-reactive aromatic anticonvulsants
Treat significant visceral involvement with systemic corticosteroids, using topical corticosteroids and emollients for cutaneous disease
Provide supportive care with fluid and electrolyte correction, temperature control, and skin barrier protection
Reserve intravenous immunoglobulin or ciclosporin for severe or corticosteroid-refractory multi-organ disease, with intensive care for fulminant hepatic, cardiac, or pulmonary failure
Monitor serial liver, renal, cardiac, and pulmonary function and test for herpesvirus (HHV-6) reactivation given its role in the relapsing course
Taper corticosteroids slowly, since flares may occur weeks after the drug is stopped
Arrange long-term follow-up for delayed autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes, and document the drug allergy prominently
